newsitem.title: LATVIA: Baltic states cheered by U.S. security initiative.
newsitem.headline: Baltic states cheered by U.S. security initiative.

text.p: The three Baltic states, anxious to establish a firm foothold in the West, hailed on Friday a U.S. initiative to speed their integration into the West's security and economic structures.

The so-called Baltic Action Plan, unveiled to Baltic diplomats in Washington on August 29, is being presented by a U.S. delegation led by U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Marshall Adair and Dan Fried of the National Security Council.
The delegation has been to Estonia and Latvia and was in Denmark on Friday ahead of a visit to the Lithuanian capital Vilnius on Saturday.
A senior U.S. diplomat told Reuters the plan was "a bilateral document in which the U.S. is encouraging the Baltic states' aspirations to integrate into NATO and other Western organisations".
Five years after quitting the former Soviet Union, the three small states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are keen to establish as close links as possible with the West.

Fearful of their large and unpredictable Russian neighbour, the Baltic states have made membership of the European Union (EU) and NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organisation) central planks of their respective foreign policies.
Many analysts and diplomats have virtually written the Baltics out of the NATO security alliance on the grounds that any link would provoke a hostile response from Moscow.
Russia has vehemently opposed NATO's plans to expand east and is particularly sensitive about the Baltics, historically part of both the Tsarist empire and the former Soviet Union.

A Lithuanian foreign ministry official told Reuters the American plan had three parts: support for Baltic bids to join NATO and the EU; improved relations with neighbouring countries, especially Russia; and bilateral support to increase U.S. investment and economic activity in the region.

Another, more senior Lithuanian foreign ministry official said: "This plan underlines the strategic importance of the Baltic states to the United States and demonstrates the American commitment to the region."
But the official, who did not want to be named, said the plan was not regarded by Lithuania as an alternative to NATO membership.
"NATO remains our top foreign policy priority," he said.

Latvian Foreign Minister Valdis Birkavs said on Thursday: "We have considered the Baltic Action Plan and voiced our concern for it not to become a substitute for NATO enlargement, and now we are sure we do not need to worry about that."
The Baltics fear they will be left out of the first wave of NATO's planned expansion and left in Russia's "sphere of influence".
